historical_timeline.summary: Born in Texas; the roster's 1925 year conflicts with current government sources.
Enlisted in the United States Army and later served in the Mediterranean and European theaters.
Wounded during the action near Holtzwihr for which he received the Medal of Honor.
Government biographies describe headaches, depression, nightmares, insomnia, and what is now called PTSD.
Died in a private-plane crash near Roanoke, Virginia.

claims.statement: Audie Leon Murphy was born June 20, 1924.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Identity fact; competing 1925 roster value retained as a conflicting assertion.

claims.statement: Murphy died May 28, 1971, in a private-plane crash near Roanoke, Virginia.
Murphy served in World War II and became one of the most decorated United States soldiers of the war.
Murphy was wounded in the leg during the January 26, 1945 action near Holtzwihr and was wounded three times during the war.
Murphy experienced postwar nightmares and insomnia.
Murphy experienced postwar depression and headaches.
Murphy's postwar symptoms are retrospectively described as post-traumatic stress disorder.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The modern diagnostic label is retrospective; the underlying symptoms are separately documented.

claims.statement: Murphy reported sleeping with a loaded pistol under his pillow.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Murphy returns six weeks after his intake visit for post-traumatic stress disorder and chronic insomnia. He has attended five weekly sessions of Cognitive Processing Therapy with Dr. Lee and completes the practice assignments between sessions; Dr. Lee's consultation report arrived today. His nightmares have fallen from most nights to two or three nights a week. He uses the agreed sleep routine on five to six nights a week and now falls asleep in about 30 minutes instead of more than an hour, although he still wakes once or twice on most nights. He startles less easily and concentrates better at work, and his mood is better. He has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm since the intake visit. He carries his safety plan, has the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline saved in his phone, and reports that the lethal-means steps agreed at intake remain in place. He drinks no alcohol, uses no cannabis or other drugs, and takes no medicines or sleep aids. No one has noticed loud snoring or pauses in his breathing, and he is not sleepy during the day.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Murphy is a 40-year-old man with post-traumatic stress disorder, much improved after completing Cognitive Processing Therapy last month, and chronic insomnia managed without medication, who asked for a same-day visit. Three days ago he developed a sore throat, followed by a runny and blocked nose and a dry cough. His highest home temperature was 37.8 °C. A home COVID-19 antigen test yesterday was negative. Several coworkers have had colds. For the past two nights the cough and blocked nose have woken him, and he is worried about losing the sleep he has regained. He had thought of buying a "nighttime" cold and flu syrup and a decongestant tablet, but wanted to check first because his care plan asks him to avoid sedating sleep aids. So far he has used only honey and throat lozenges. He has no breathlessness, chest pain, ear pain, or facial pain. His nightmares have not increased, his mood is steady, and he has had no thoughts of self-harm.

referral.question: Chronic combat-related post-traumatic stress symptoms in a 40-year-old veteran, with chronic insomnia and depressive symptoms. Please confirm the diagnosis, provide trauma-focused psychotherapy, and advise on sleep, the depressive symptoms, and suicide risk
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks. No current suicidal ideation, intent, or plan; a collaborative safety plan was completed today
referral.pertinent_history: Long-standing nightmares on most nights, trouble falling and staying asleep, hypervigilance, a strong startle, avoidance of crowds, and low mood since his combat service, with poor concentration at work. PCL-5 42 and PHQ-9 11 today. No current thoughts of suicide, intent, or plan. Access to lethal means was reviewed, and a collaborative safety and lethal-means plan with crisis resources, including the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, was completed today. No alcohol in the past year, no tobacco or drugs, and no medicines. He prefers to start with psychotherapy rather than medication. Strengths: family and veteran peer supports, purposeful work, and a strong service identity
questions: Does he meet criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder, and are the depressive symptoms part of it or a separate depressive disorder?
Is he a good candidate for trauma-focused psychotherapy such as Cognitive Processing Therapy, and can your service provide it?
How should the insomnia and nightmares be treated before any sleep medication is considered?
What is your formulation of his suicide risk, and do you have any changes to the safety plan?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Murphy was referred by Dr. Marquez at his intake visit six weeks ago. I evaluated him at the start of care and have since delivered five weekly sessions of Cognitive Processing Therapy; this report answers the referral questions. He describes intrusive memories and nightmares of combat, avoidance of reminders and crowds, beliefs about blame and constant danger, and hypervigilance with a strong startle, present for many years and made worse by poor sleep. He engages well and completes the practice assignments. Since starting therapy his nightmares have fallen from most nights to two or three a week, he falls asleep sooner with the agreed sleep routine, and he concentrates better at work. He has had no thoughts of suicide, intent, plan, or preparatory behavior since intake and keeps the safety plan with him. He uses no alcohol, drugs, or medicines. He has had no manic or hypomanic episodes and no psychotic symptoms
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Marquez's intake note and safety plan, the intake PCL-5 and PHQ-9, today's repeat scores, and his therapy practice assignments

exam.finding: Well groomed; cooperative with good eye contact; briefly restless when describing nightmares
Normal rate, volume, and rhythm
Mood "better than in June"; affect mildly anxious, reactive, and less constricted than at intake
Linear and goal directed; no suicidal or homicidal ideation, intent, or plan; no delusions
No hallucinations; no dissociation during the session
Alert and fully oriented; attention and recall intact
Good

assessment.assessment: Confirmed on clinical interview against DSM-5-TR criteria, with intrusion, avoidance, negative changes in thinking and mood, and arousal symptoms all present at evaluation. He is responding to Cognitive Processing Therapy: the PCL-5 fell 11 points, from 42 to 31, a clinically meaningful change, but 31 is still near the probable-PTSD range, so the full course should be completed

The low mood, poor sleep, and poor concentration track the PTSD symptoms and are improving with them (PHQ-9 11 to 7). There is no separate major depressive episode on interview and no history of mania or hypomania, so no separate depressive disorder is diagnosed and a bipolar screen is not needed
Improving with the sleep routine, used on five to six nights a week, and with the trauma-focused work. He reports no snoring, witnessed apneas, or daytime sleepiness

Acute risk is low: no current ideation, intent, plan, or preparatory behavior; active engagement in treatment; and strong protective factors in his family and peer supports, purposeful work, and service identity. Chronic risk is higher than in the general population because of combat exposure, PTSD, and chronic insomnia. The collaborative safety and lethal-means plan from intake is appropriate and needs no change. Outpatient care is appropriate

recommendations: Complete the Cognitive Processing Therapy course, with a goal of at least eight sessions by the twelve-week review
No PTSD medication at present, given his preference and his response; reconsider only if the response stalls
Continue the sleep routine and stimulus control; offer cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia if the insomnia persists after the course; no sleep medication now
Avoid benzodiazepines and over-the-counter sedating sleep aids
No separate depression treatment; repeat the PHQ-9 with the PCL-5 at the twelve-week review
Review the safety plan at each primary-care visit and therapy session, keeping the lethal-means steps and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line) in place
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Marquez today; Mr. Murphy agrees with the plan and has a copy of this report
consultant_note.follow_up: Weekly Cognitive Processing Therapy with me to the end of the course, then booster sessions as needed. Primary care repeats the PCL-5 and PHQ-9 at the twelve-week review. I will see him sooner for any suicidal thoughts or a stall in progress
